title: The Long Family Tree
subtitle: How life changes, how we know, and where you fit in
subject: Biology

pages.h: Every living thing is your cousin
p: The oak outside, the mould on old bread, the bacteria in your gut, the fly on the window, and you: all of you descend from a single population of cells that lived about 4 billion years ago. Biologists call that ancestor LUCA, the last universal common ancestor. Nobody has a fossil of it. We know it existed because of what every living thing has in common.

All life on Earth stores its instructions in DNA, using the same four chemical letters. All of it reads those instructions with the same code, where the same three-letter words mean the same building blocks. All of it runs on the same energy molecule, ATP. If life had started more than once, we would expect to find at least one creature that does things differently. We never have.

The family resemblance goes deeper than you might like. Your DNA is about 98.8 percent identical to a chimpanzee's. About 85 percent of your genes have a clear match in a mouse. Roughly 60 percent have a recognisable version in a fruit fly. Even yeast, the single-celled fungus that makes bread rise, shares hundreds of genes with you so similar that scientists have swapped the human version into yeast and watched it work.
This book is about how one ancestor became millions of kinds of living things, how we know, and why it matters.
pages.cap: The first cells divided, and divided again. Every living thing today is a branch from that start.
pages.fact: Did you know? About 8 percent of your DNA comes from ancient viruses that infected your ancestors and never left.

pages.h: Variation: no two are the same
p: Look around a classroom. Nobody is identical, not even twins once life has worked on them for a while. The same is true for every species. No two sparrows, no two oak trees, no two bacteria in a colony are exactly alike. This variation is the raw material of evolution, and it comes from two main sources.

The first is mixing. When parents reproduce, their genes are shuffled into new combinations. Your genes are half from each parent, but the half you got is a random deal, and a brother or sister gets a different deal.

The second is mutation. Every time a cell copies its 3.2 billion letters of DNA, it makes a few mistakes. Each of us is born with about 60 to 70 new mutations that neither parent had. Most land in parts of the DNA that do nothing in particular and have no effect. A few are harmful. Very occasionally one is useful: it makes an enzyme slightly faster, a feather slightly stiffer, a leaf slightly better at catching light.

Mutation is random. It has no idea what the organism needs. That is the part people find hardest to accept, and it is also the key to the whole thing. Evolution does not need mutation to be clever. It only needs it to be varied, and then something else does the choosing.
pages.cap: Every person carries about 60 new mutations that neither parent had. Variation is the raw material.
pages.fact: Did you know? Any two humans differ at roughly 3 million DNA letters, about one letter in a thousand.

pages.h: A drought, a finch, and 4 percent
p: On a tiny island in the Galapagos called Daphne Major, two biologists, Peter and Rosemary Grant, measured every single finch for 40 years. Every bird was banded. Every beak was measured to a tenth of a millimetre. Then, in 1977, almost no rain fell.

The plants that make small, soft seeds died off. What was left were big, hard seeds that only the birds with the deepest, strongest beaks could crack. About 85 percent of the medium ground finches on the island starved. The survivors were not random. Their beaks were, on average, about 4 percent deeper than the beaks of the birds that died.

Beak depth is inherited. The next year, the chicks of the survivors had deeper beaks than the chicks born before the drought. In a single generation, the population had changed. Then in 1983 heavy rains came, small seeds were plentiful, and the advantage swung back toward smaller beaks. The Grants watched the population move back the other way.

Charles Darwin had visited these islands in 1835 and guessed that something like this must happen. He thought it would be far too slow to see. The Grants proved him right about the process and wrong about the speed. Evolution is not only something that happened in the deep past. It is happening on Daphne Major this year.
pages.cap: After the drought killed most of the finches, the survivors and their chicks had measurably deeper beaks.

p: Darwin's idea is simple enough to fit in four lines, and that simplicity is why it is so powerful.

One: individuals vary. Two: some of that variation is inherited. Three: more offspring are born than can possibly survive. Four: therefore, whichever variations help survival and reproduction, even slightly, become more common with each generation. Darwin called this natural selection. Nature does not choose on purpose. Some variations simply leave more copies of themselves.

Step three is the engine. A female cod can lay 9 million eggs in a season. If all of them lived and bred, the ocean would be solid cod within a few years. On average, in a stable population, just two survive to replace their parents. The other 8,999,998 die, and which ones die is not entirely luck.

People often sum this up as 'survival of the fittest', and then misunderstand it. Fittest does not mean strongest or fastest. It means best fitted to the local conditions right now. In a drought, a slightly deeper beak. In a sooty city, a slightly darker wing. In a cold sea, a slightly thicker layer of fat. Small advantages, over thousands of generations, add up to new kinds of creatures. No step requires anything but time, variation, and the plain fact that not everyone makes it.
pages.cap: Every link in a food chain is under pressure. Rabbits that hear a fox a little sooner leave more baby rabbits.

pages.h: A whale's flipper, a bat's wing and your hand have the same bones
p: One upper arm bone, two forearm bones, a cluster of wrist bones, five fingers. Stretched, shortened or fused, the same set appears in every mammal, bird, reptile and amphibian. It is the signature of a shared ancestor that lived about 370 million years ago.

pages.q: In 1977 a drought on Daphne Major left only big, hard seeds. What happened to the finches?
opts: They all grew bigger beaks to cope
Birds that already had deeper beaks survived more often and passed the trait on
pages.why: Individuals cannot change their beaks. Selection acted on variation that already existed: deep-beaked birds survived and bred.

p: Every dog on Earth, from a Chihuahua to a Great Dane, descends from grey wolves. Humans did the selecting instead of nature, and it worked frighteningly fast. Scientists argue about when it began, with estimates between 15,000 and 40,000 years ago, but most of the breeds you know are less than 200 years old.

The process is the same as natural selection, with people as the drought. Breeders pick the puppies with the traits they like, and only those puppies get to breed. Repeat for a few dozen generations and you have a dachshund. Darwin opened his famous book with pigeon breeding for exactly this reason: if people could reshape an animal that much in a few centuries, what could nature do in millions of years?

A Russian scientist named Dmitry Belyaev tested it directly. Starting in 1959, he bred silver foxes, choosing only the least fearful from each litter. Within about ten generations some foxes wagged their tails and licked hands. Within forty they had floppy ears, curly tails and spotted coats, traits no one had selected for but which came along with tameness. The experiment is still running.

Plants went through the same thing. Maize was bred from a scraggly Mexican grass called teosinte, with cobs the size of your little finger, about 9,000 years ago. A modern cob is 15 times bigger. Every food you eat is an evolution experiment that humans ran.

v.title: Humans as selectors
items: Darwin publishes On the Origin of Species

pages.cap: People have been directing evolution for at least 10,000 years, long before anyone knew what it was.

p: Most living things vanish without a trace. They rot, get eaten, or dissolve. A fossil needs luck: a body buried quickly in mud, sand or ash before scavengers and bacteria finish with it. Over thousands of years, minerals seep in and replace bone with stone, or leave a hollow in the rock the exact shape of the creature. Fewer than one in a million animals that ever lived left a fossil we have found.

Despite that, museums hold millions of them, and they fall into a pattern. Layers of rock stack up over time, so lower layers are older. Deep layers hold only simple sea creatures. Higher up come fish, then amphibians, then reptiles, then mammals and birds. Nobody has ever found a rabbit fossil in a 500-million-year-old layer. If someone did, the whole theory would be in trouble. It has not happened.

Canada holds one of the world's greatest fossil sites. The Burgess Shale, in Yoho National Park in British Columbia, preserves soft-bodied sea animals from 508 million years ago, so perfectly that you can see their guts and the hairs on their legs. Alberta's badlands hold some of the richest dinosaur beds anywhere. Nova Scotia's Joggins cliffs show whole fossil forests from 310 million years ago. The story of life is written in Canadian rock.
pages.cap: Each layer is a page. The deeper you dig, the older the page, and the simpler the life it holds.
pages.fact: Did you know? A dinosaur footprint is a fossil too. A single site in Bolivia has more than 5,000 of them on one cliff face.

p: If fish really did evolve into animals with legs, there should once have been a creature halfway between. It should have lived about 375 million years ago, because older rocks hold only fish and younger rocks hold four-legged animals. And it should be found in rock that was once a shallow river, laid down at that time.

A team led by Neil Shubin looked at a geology map, found rock of exactly that age on Ellesmere Island in Nunavut, and went looking. It took four summers in the Arctic. In 2004 they found it: a flat-headed fish up to 2.7 metres long with scales and fins, but also a neck, ribs, lungs, and, inside its fins, the bones of a wrist, an elbow and a shoulder. Elders in Nunavut named it Tiktaalik, meaning a large freshwater fish.

Tiktaalik could prop itself up in shallow water and probably haul itself through the weeds like a seal. It was not our direct ancestor, any more than your great-great-aunt is. It was a cousin, showing what the family looked like at that stage.

The point is not just that a halfway animal exists. It is that scientists said where and when it should be found, and then found it there. A theory that makes that kind of prediction, and gets it right, has earned trust.
pages.cap: Tiktaalik was found in rock layers of exactly the predicted age, 375 million years old, in Nunavut.

p: For the first 3 billion years, life on Earth was mostly tiny: single cells, mats of bacteria, and, near the end, some soft blobby animals with no heads, legs or shells. Then, about 538 million years ago, almost every major group of animals alive today appeared in the fossil record within about 20 million years. Biologists call it the Cambrian explosion.

Twenty million years is not fast on a human scale. But against 3 billion years of slime, it is a sprint. Suddenly there were animals with eyes, legs, jaws, shells and spines. The Burgess Shale in British Columbia preserves them in startling detail: five-eyed Opabinia with a trunk like a vacuum hose, Hallucigenia walking on stilts with spikes on its back, and Anomalocaris, a predator up to a metre long with grasping arms and a mouth like a camera shutter.

What set it off? Scientists argue about this. Oxygen levels rose around then, making bigger, more active bodies possible. The first eyes may have started an arms race between hunters and hunted, where shells and speed suddenly paid off. New genes for building body plans had evolved. Most likely all three mattered.

Nearly every animal alive today, including you, belongs to a group that first shows up in the Cambrian. Your basic body plan, with a head, a gut running front to back and a nerve cord along your back, was already being tried out in those seas.
pages.cap: Cambrian seas were full of experiments. Most of these body plans died out; a few became everything alive today.

p: Natural selection is easy to see when you are the one doing the selecting.
steps: Get about 20 coloured toothpicks or short pieces of yarn in each of five colours: green, brown, red, yellow and blue. That is 100 'insects'.
Have a friend scatter them over a patch of grass or a leafy garden bed while you look away.
You are a hungry bird. Give yourself 30 seconds to pick up as many as you can, one at a time. Then stop.
Count the survivors by colour. Which colours did you miss most? Those are the camouflaged ones.
Now let each survivor 'breed': for every survivor, add one more of the same colour. Scatter them all again and repeat for three or four rounds.

Write down the colour counts after each round. After a few generations the population should be mostly the colours that match the background. Nobody told the insects to change. The ones that stood out got eaten.
pages.cap: A moth that matches its tree lives to lay eggs. Over generations, the whole population shifts toward the colour that hides best.
pages.safe: Pick up every toothpick at the end so animals and bare feet do not find them.

p: Before 1848 nearly every peppered moth in England was pale and speckled, and nearly invisible against the lichen-covered bark it rested on. That year a black one was caught near Manchester. By 1895, 98 percent of the peppered moths around Manchester were black.

The reason was soot. Coal smoke from factories killed the pale lichens and blackened the trees. A pale moth on a black trunk was lunch. A black moth was hidden. Birds did the selecting, and the colour of a whole species flipped in less than 50 years.
Then the story ran in reverse. After clean-air laws in the 1950s and 1960s, the soot cleared, lichens grew back, and the black form faded. Today it is rare again.

Some critics claimed the original experiments, done in the 1950s by placing moths on trunks, were flawed. So between 2001 and 2007 a biologist named Michael Majerus watched 4,864 moths in his own garden, over seven years, and confirmed that birds ate far more of the poorly matched ones. In 2016 geneticists found the exact mutation that made the black form: a piece of jumping DNA that landed in a gene called cortex, around the year 1819. One moth, one mutation, one changed city, and the whole species followed.
pages.cap: Soot from coal fires turned the trees black, and within 50 years the moths followed.
pages.fact: Did you know? The same kind of darkening happened to ladybirds, spiders and pigeons in sooty cities.

p: A whale is a mammal. It breathes air, is warm-blooded, and feeds its young milk. Its flipper has the bones of a hand. Deep in a modern whale's body, with no connection to anything, float two small bones that are the remains of hips. A whale is a land animal that went back to the sea, and the fossils show every step.

Fifty million years ago, in what is now Pakistan, lived Pakicetus, a wolf-sized animal with hooves, a long snout, and a peculiar thick ear bone found only in whales today. It waded. Two million years later came Ambulocetus, built like a 3-metre crocodile with big webbed feet, hunting in river mouths. Then Rodhocetus, with shrinking legs and a strengthening tail. Then, around 40 million years ago, Basilosaurus, a 17-metre sea serpent with tiny hind legs the length of your forearm, useless for walking.

Each of these was found after Darwin's theory predicted that such creatures should exist, and each shows the same trend: nostrils migrating up the skull to become a blowhole, legs shrinking, tail growing a fluke. DNA confirms the story from the other direction. The whale's closest living relative is the hippopotamus.
Occasionally a modern whale is born with small hind limbs sticking out of its body. The genes to build legs are still in there, switched off, waiting.

v.title: From wader to giant in 50 million years

pages.cap: Pakicetus waded in rivers 50 million years ago. Its descendants include the largest animal that has ever lived.

pages.q: Which fact is evidence that whales descend from land mammals?
opts: Whales have tiny leftover hip bones and hand bones inside their flippers
pages.why: Leftover hips and hand bones make no sense for an animal that has always lived in water, but make perfect sense for one whose ancestors walked.

pages.h: DNA: the recipe in every cell
p: Inside almost every one of your 37 trillion cells sits a copy of the same instruction book. It is written in DNA, a molecule shaped like a twisted ladder, with rungs made of four chemical letters: A, T, C and G. Your copy is about 3.2 billion letters long. Printed in a normal font, it would fill 200 phone books. Stretched out, the DNA from one cell is about 2 metres long, coiled into a space smaller than a speck of dust.

Stretches of that text called genes, about 20,000 of them, carry the instructions for building proteins, the molecules that do nearly everything in a body. Most of the rest of your DNA controls when and where those genes are switched on, or does nothing anyone has yet understood.

When a cell divides, it copies the whole book. When you have a child, half of your book is combined with half of your partner's. That is how traits are inherited, and that is where evolution happens: in the changes that creep into the text as it is copied over and over for billions of years.

Darwin never knew about DNA. He had no idea how traits were passed on, and he said so. When the structure of DNA was worked out in 1953, it could have proven him wrong. Instead it explained exactly how his idea worked, and then added evidence he never dreamed of.
pages.cap: A twisted ladder of four letters. Every creature on Earth uses the same alphabet and the same code.

p: If two species share a recent ancestor, their DNA should be nearly identical. If their ancestor is distant, their DNA should have had more time to drift apart. So you can draw a family tree from DNA alone, without a single fossil, and then check it against the fossils. The two trees match.

Humans and chimpanzees differ at about 1.2 percent of their DNA letters. Humans and gorillas, about 1.6 percent. Humans and orangutans, about 3 percent. Humans and mice, around 15 percent in the genes that line up. The DNA says we split from chimps roughly 6 to 7 million years ago, and the oldest human-like fossils are, sure enough, about that old.

There is a scar in your DNA that tells the same story. Chimps, gorillas and orangutans have 24 pairs of chromosomes. Humans have 23. Where did one go? Look at human chromosome 2: it is exactly what you would get by sticking two ape chromosomes end to end. In the middle, where the join happened, sit the leftover caps that normally only appear at chromosome ends, and a second, disabled centre point. Two chromosomes fused in an ancestor of ours, and every human alive carries the seam.
Scientists argue about the details: exactly when the splits happened, and whether early humans and chimps interbred for a while after. But the shape of the tree is not in doubt.

v.title: All humans: 99.9 percent the same DNA

pages.cap: Any two people differ by about one DNA letter in a thousand. A person and a chimp differ by about twelve.

pages.h: The broken gene for vitamin C
p: Most animals make their own vitamin C. A dog, a cow, a rat: none needs it in their food, because a gene called GULO builds the enzyme that makes it. You cannot. Neither can a chimpanzee, a gorilla, or a monkey. Without vitamin C in your diet you get scurvy, which killed about two million sailors in the age of sail.

Here is the strange part. You still have the GULO gene. It is sitting in your DNA, in the same place as in a rat, and it is broken, riddled with mutations that stop it working. Chimps and gorillas have the same broken gene, with the same breaks in the same places. That is exactly what you would expect if the gene broke once, in a shared ancestor that ate plenty of fruit and never missed it, and every descendant inherited the wreck.

Guinea pigs also cannot make vitamin C. Their GULO gene is broken too, but with completely different mutations. Their copy failed separately, on its own branch of the tree. If a designer had built each species from scratch, there would be no reason to install a broken part. If each species inherited its DNA from its ancestors, broken parts are exactly what you would expect.
Your DNA holds about 20,000 of these dead genes, called pseudogenes. Many are old scent receptors, from when our ancestors relied on smell. Each is a fossil in the text.
pages.cap: Inside every one of your cells is a gene for making vitamin C. It stopped working about 60 million years ago.

p: At four weeks old, a human embryo has a tail, with a dozen tiny vertebrae in it. It has a row of folds along its neck, in the same positions where a fish embryo develops gill slits. A bit later, it grows a thin coat of fur all over, called lanugo, and then sheds it before birth. None of these features makes much sense unless you know where we came from.

The tail usually shrinks into the tailbone, a small set of fused bones at the base of your spine that you can feel if you press. The neck folds become your jaw, ear bones, voice box and the glands in your throat. In a fish, the same folds become gills. In you, they are rebuilt into something else, because evolution does not start over. It edits what is already there.

Whale embryos grow hind limb buds and then reabsorb them. Snake embryos briefly start to build legs. Chickens carry the genes to grow teeth, and in the lab, scientists have switched them on and watched tooth buds form in a chick's beak.

An old slogan said embryos replay their evolutionary history as they develop. That is not quite right, and biologists argue over how much embryos really tell us. But the basic point stands: development follows an old program, and the program carries edits on top of edits going back half a billion years.
pages.cap: A human heart starts as a simple tube, like a fish heart, and then folds and divides into four chambers.

pages.h: For most of life's history, life was single-celled
p: The oldest fossils are about 3.5 billion years old. Animals big enough to see appeared only about 600 million years ago. If Earth's history were one day, complex life shows up around 9 p.m., dinosaurs at about 10:45, and our species in the last 6 seconds before midnight.

pages.q: Humans, chimps and gorillas all have the same broken vitamin C gene, with the same breaks. What is the best explanation?
opts: Fruit-eating animals always break this gene the same way
The gene broke once in a shared ancestor and all three inherited it
pages.why: Identical breaks in the same places are the signature of inheritance from a common ancestor. Guinea pigs broke theirs separately, with different mutations.

p: Extinction is normal. Species usually last a few million years and then disappear, replaced by others. But at least five times in the last 500 million years, something went badly wrong and most of life vanished in a geological instant. Scientists call these the Big Five mass extinctions.

The worst was 252 million years ago, at the end of the Permian period. Over a few tens of thousands of years, somewhere between 80 and 96 percent of species in the ocean died, along with most on land. Geologists call it the Great Dying. The main suspect is a vast outpouring of lava in what is now Siberia, which burned through coal beds and pumped out so much carbon dioxide that the oceans heated, turned acidic and lost their oxygen. Life took about 10 million years to recover.

The others: about 445 million years ago, when the climate swung cold then hot. About 372 million years ago, when the oceans lost oxygen again. About 201 million years ago, more giant volcanoes, which cleared the way for dinosaurs to dominate. And 66 million years ago, the one everyone knows.

Each time, the survivors inherited an emptied world and evolution ran wild filling it. Mass extinction is a tragedy for the species that die and an opportunity for the ones that do not. Mammals, including you, owe their rise to one.
pages.cap: Volcanoes on the scale of a continent, erupting for a million years, caused the biggest extinction of all.
pages.fact: Did you know? Some scientists argue that a sixth mass extinction has begun, caused by humans. Others say the numbers are not yet in that league. The disagreement is about scale, not about whether species are being lost.

p: Sixty-six million years ago, a rock about 10 kilometres across, the size of a mountain, hit the sea near what is now the Yucatan Peninsula in Mexico at about 20 kilometres per second. It blasted a crater 180 kilometres wide and threw molten rock across the planet. Within hours the falling debris heated the sky like a grill. Then dust and sulfur blotted out the Sun for years. Plants died, then the animals that ate them, then the animals that ate those. About 75 percent of species disappeared, including every dinosaur that was not a bird.

How do we know? In 1980 a father and son team, Luis and Walter Alvarez, found a thin clay layer in rocks of exactly that age, all over the world, rich in iridium, a metal rare on Earth but common in asteroids. The crater itself, named Chicxulub, was confirmed in 1991. In North Dakota, a site called Tanis preserves fish with impact glass in their gills, killed within an hour.
Scientists still argue about the details. Giant volcanic eruptions in India were already stressing the climate, and some think they deserve part of the blame. But the asteroid was the final blow.

It was the best day in history for mammals. For 150 million years they had been small, mostly nocturnal, and kept down by dinosaurs. Within a few hundred thousand years they were growing and spreading, heading for whales, bats and us.
pages.cap: A 10-kilometre asteroid struck 66 million years ago. The dinosaurs' loss was the mammals' chance.
pages.fact: Did you know? Birds are living dinosaurs. A chicken is more closely related to Tyrannosaurus than Tyrannosaurus was to Stegosaurus.

pages.h: Why extinction is part of the story
p: Of every species that has ever lived on Earth, more than 99 percent are extinct. That is not a failure of the system. It is the system. Evolution works by trying out variations and keeping the ones that fit the moment. When the moment changes, the fit changes, and species that were perfect for the old world vanish.

Dinosaurs ruled for about 165 million years, far longer than mammals have so far. They were not a mistake. They were extremely good at being dinosaurs, right up until the conditions they were good at stopped existing. The same is true of trilobites, which filled the seas for 270 million years, and of giant dragonflies with 70-centimetre wingspans, and of the sabre-toothed cats that hunted in what is now Alberta until about 11,000 years ago.

Normal, background extinction runs at roughly one species per million species per year. Today, by most estimates, the rate is 100 to 1,000 times that, driven by habitat loss, hunting, introduced species and a changing climate. Scientists argue about the exact multiplier, because we do not even know how many species there are. Estimates range from 8 million to far more. But nearly all agree the current rate is far above background.
That matters because recovery after a mass extinction takes millions of years. Whatever disappears now will not be back on any timescale that means anything to people.
pages.cap: Sauropods were the largest land animals ever, and they lasted 140 million years. Nothing lasts forever.

p: Our branch split from the chimpanzee branch about 6 to 7 million years ago in Africa. For most of the time since, there were several kinds of human-like creatures alive at once. We are the only one left, which makes our lineage look like a single straight line. It was a bush.

In 1974 a skeleton nicknamed Lucy was found in Ethiopia: 3.2 million years old, 1.1 metres tall, with a chimp-sized brain, but hips and knees built for walking upright. Walking came first; big brains came much later. By about 1.5 million years ago, Homo erectus had a bigger brain, made stone tools, probably controlled fire, and had walked out of Africa all the way to what is now Indonesia.

Our own species, Homo sapiens, appears in the fossil record about 300,000 years ago in Morocco. When our ancestors spread out of Africa around 60,000 years ago, they met other humans already living in Europe and Asia: Neanderthals, and a group called Denisovans known mostly from DNA. We did not just meet. Almost everyone whose ancestors left Africa carries 1 to 2 percent Neanderthal DNA today. People in Papua New Guinea carry up to 5 percent Denisovan.

Neanderthals vanished about 40,000 years ago. Scientists argue about why: competition, climate, disease, small numbers, or simply being absorbed into our much larger population. Whatever happened, a bit of them is reading this sentence.
pages.cap: For most of the last 2 million years, more than one kind of human shared the planet. Now there is one.

p: Every baby mammal drinks milk, and every baby mammal makes an enzyme called lactase to digest the milk sugar, lactose. In nearly all mammals, and in most humans, the lactase gene switches off after weaning. Drink milk as an adult and you get cramps and worse. That is the original condition. About 65 percent of adults on Earth today still have it.

Then, starting around 10,000 years ago, people in a few places began herding cattle, goats and camels. In those populations, a mutation that kept the lactase gene switched on into adulthood became hugely valuable: a safe, year-round source of calories that nobody else could use. It spread fast. In Denmark today, around 95 percent of adults digest milk easily. In China, about 5 percent. The mutation arose at least four separate times, in Europe, Arabia and twice in East Africa, each time among herders.

This is natural selection acting on humans in the recent past, and it is still in your genes. If you can drink a glass of milk without trouble, you carry a mutation that spread because some ancestor of yours kept cows.

Other examples are piling up. Tibetans breathe easily at 4,000 metres because of a gene variant that came from Denisovans. Some West African populations carry a gene that protects against malaria at the cost of sickle-cell disease. Humans have not stopped evolving. We have only stopped noticing.
pages.cap: Rough shares of adults who can digest milk. The pattern follows thousands of years of herding history.

pages.h: Try it: build a family tree from features
p: Biologists build evolutionary trees by grouping species that share features inherited from a common ancestor. You can do it with a deck of cards.
steps: Write each of these animals on its own card: shark, salmon, frog, lizard, pigeon, mouse, dolphin, bat, human.
Make a feature list: backbone, jaws, four limbs, lays eggs with shells or gives live birth, feathers, fur, feeds young milk, can fly, lives in water.
For each feature, sort the cards into has it and does not have it. Write the results in a grid.
Now group. Everything has a backbone and jaws, so that is the base. Only the shark and salmon lack four limbs, so they branch off first. Fur and milk group mouse, dolphin, bat and human together.
Draw the tree with the base at the bottom and branches splitting where features appear.

Notice the traps. Dolphin and salmon both live in water, but the tree says dolphin belongs with the mammals. Bat and pigeon both fly, but they got wings separately. Features that evolve more than once are what make real trees hard, and DNA is how scientists settle the arguments.
pages.cap: Sorting by shared features is how biologists draw family trees. Shared shape can mislead; shared ancestry does not.

pages.q: Almost everyone whose ancestors left Africa carries 1 to 2 percent Neanderthal DNA. What does that tell us?
opts: Our ancestors and Neanderthals met and had children together
pages.why: Neanderthals were a separate human branch. The DNA shows the two groups interbred before the Neanderthal line disappeared about 40,000 years ago.

p: Bacteria can divide every 20 minutes. That means a single cell can become a billion in a day, and each division is a chance for a mutation. When you fill that population with an antibiotic, almost every cell dies. Almost. If one in a billion happens to carry a mutation that lets it survive, then tomorrow the whole population descends from that one, and the antibiotic no longer works.

This is natural selection at a speed you can watch. In 1988 a biologist named Richard Lenski put E. coli bacteria into 12 flasks of weak sugar water and let them grow, transferring a sample to a fresh flask every day. The experiment has now run for more than 80,000 generations. The bacteria have grown bigger, reproduce faster, and in 2003 one flask did something astonishing: its bacteria evolved the ability to eat citrate, a chemical E. coli had never been able to use. Lenski froze samples every 500 generations, so he can thaw the ancestors and replay the tape.

The cost in hospitals is enormous. In 2019, infections by bacteria that had evolved resistance to antibiotics directly killed about 1.27 million people worldwide, more than malaria or HIV. Every unnecessary course of antibiotics, every dose not finished, is a selection experiment that breeds tougher germs.
Evolution is not something that only happens to other species over millions of years. It happens inside hospitals, inside your body, this week.
pages.cap: One bacterium in a billion survives the drug. A day later, its descendants are the whole population.

p: Cities are a new kind of habitat, and living things are already adapting to them, fast enough for scientists to measure.

In Puerto Rico, lizards called crested anoles that live on buildings have longer legs and stickier toe pads than those in nearby forests, better for gripping smooth concrete and glass. In Nebraska, cliff swallows that nest on highway bridges have evolved wings about 4 millimetres shorter over 30 years, which lets them take off faster and dodge cars. The roadkill count fell as the wings shrank. In 2022 a team measured white clover in 160 cities on six continents and found that city clover had repeatedly lost the ability to make a cyanide defence, because the pests it protects against are rarer among buildings.

A famous example is the London Underground mosquito, long described as a species that evolved in the subway tunnels after they opened in 1863. Genetic work published in 2024 suggests this form is actually thousands of years old and came from the Middle East. Scientists are arguing about it right now, which is a good reminder that popular stories need checking.

Cities select for boldness, for tolerance of noise and light, for eating human food. Urban foxes, coyotes and crows are measurably different from their country relatives. Whatever lives in a city 10,000 years from now will be shaped by what we are building today.
pages.cap: Shorter wings mean faster take-off. Swallows that nest by highways have evolved them in a few decades.

pages.h: Fish that shrank and elephants without tusks
p: People are now the strongest selecting force on Earth, and we often select without meaning to.

For centuries, fishing fleets off Newfoundland took the biggest Atlantic cod. A cod that grew slowly and bred young, while still small, was more likely to pass on its genes before the net got it. Over decades the fish evolved to mature earlier and smaller. When the cod population collapsed in 1992 and fishing was banned, the fish did not simply grow back to the old size. Evolution had moved, and it does not reverse on command.

In Gorongosa National Park in Mozambique, a civil war from 1977 to 1992 brought heavy ivory poaching. Elephants with tusks were shot; a few females born without tusks, a rare natural condition, were spared. Before the war, about 18 percent of adult females were tuskless. Among females born during it, about 33 percent were. In 2021 researchers found the genes responsible. One of them is lethal to male embryos, which is why the tuskless elephants are female. In a single generation, hunting had reshaped a species.

The same thing has happened to bighorn sheep with smaller horns in trophy-hunted areas, to elephants in Asia, and to wild plants in heavily mowed parks that now flower shorter and faster. Whenever humans kill some and spare others by a rule, the survivors' children follow the rule.
pages.cap: Fishing takes the biggest fish, year after year. Fish that breed early and small inherit the sea.

pages.h: Evolution has no goal. It cannot see ahead.
p: It keeps whatever works right now, and throws away the rest. It cannot plan for next century. It cannot aim for humans. It is not a ladder with us at the top. It is a bush, and every living thing is at the tip of a branch that has survived just as long as yours.

'It is only a theory.' In everyday speech a theory is a guess. In science a theory is the highest rank an idea can reach: an explanation tested so many ways, by so many people, that it would take extraordinary evidence to overturn it. Gravity is a theory. Germs causing disease is a theory. Evolution sits in that company.
'Humans came from monkeys.' No. Humans and today's monkeys are cousins who share an ancestor, the way you and your cousin share a grandparent. You did not come from your cousin.

'Evolution is random.' Mutation is random. Selection is the opposite of random. It keeps what works, consistently, generation after generation. A random process could not have produced an eye. A random source of variation plus a non-random filter did.
'Individuals evolve.' No individual changes its genes during its life. Populations change, as some individuals leave more descendants than others.

'Evolution makes things better.' It makes things better suited to their current surroundings, which is not the same. A tapeworm, which has lost its gut, eyes and most of its brain, is superbly evolved for living inside another animal.
'If evolution were true, we would see it.' We do. Finches, moths, bacteria, cod, elephants, clover. This book has shown you eight examples measured within a human lifetime.
pages.cap: Humans and chimpanzees are cousins. Neither came from the other. Both came from an ancestor that was neither.

p: That evolution happened, and that natural selection drives much of it, is not in scientific dispute. Plenty else is, and the arguments are where the interesting work is.

How did life start? Nobody knows. Some think the first self-copying molecules formed in warm pools on land, with wet and dry cycles. Others favour hot vents on the deep sea floor. Experiments can make the building blocks of life in both settings, but no one has made life.

How fast does evolution usually go? Some biologists see long stretches of little change interrupted by bursts, a pattern called punctuated equilibrium. Others see steady change that the fossil record only looks jumpy because fossils are rare.

How much change is selection, and how much is luck? In small populations, a trait can spread simply by chance, a process called drift. How much of the difference between species is drift rather than selection is hotly debated.

Can experiences be inherited? For a century the answer was no. Now there is evidence that some chemical tags on DNA, which switch genes on or off, can occasionally pass to children. How common and how important this is divides researchers sharply.

Why did Neanderthals vanish? Why did the Cambrian explosion happen when it did? What killed the Permian? Each has several camps. If you want a career where people are still fighting over the answers, this is one.
pages.cap: How life began is one of the biggest open questions in science. Several ideas compete; none has won.

p: Evolution is not just a story about the past. It is a tool people use every day, and understanding it can protect your life.

Every autumn the flu vaccine is remade, because the flu virus evolves so fast that last year's version no longer matches. Scientists track mutations around the world and predict, months ahead, which strains will dominate. Sometimes they guess wrong, and the vaccine works less well. That is an evolution forecast, made and checked every year.

Doctors now prescribe antibiotics more carefully, and ask you to finish the course, because they are thinking about selection in the bacteria in your body. Cancer is evolution inside you: cells that mutate to grow without limit, and then evolve resistance to drugs. New treatments are designed with that in mind.

Farmers rotate crops and pesticides so that pests cannot adapt to one. Plant breeders use evolutionary thinking to produce wheat that survives drought and rice that survives floods. Conservation biologists plan wildlife corridors so that populations stay large enough to keep evolving.

And there is the plain wonder of it. You are standing at the tip of an unbroken line of ancestors, every one of which survived long enough to reproduce, going back 4 billion years without a single gap. So is the fly on the window. That is a strange and rather wonderful thing to have in common.
pages.cap: Every crop in a field is the result of selection, by farmers for thousands of years and by scientists today.

a change in DNA; the source of new variation, and random
the process by which traits that help survival and reproduction become more common
a feature shaped by natural selection that fits a creature to its surroundings
the preserved remains or traces of a living thing, usually turned to stone
a species from which two or more later species descend
the molecule that carries the instructions for building a living thing, in four chemical letters
a stretch of DNA that carries the instructions for one protein or one job
a broken gene that no longer works but is still carried in the DNA
an event in which a large share of all species die out in a short time
a group of living things that can breed with each other and produce fertile young

qs: Humans now shape the evolution of cod, elephants, bacteria and clover without meaning to. Do we have a responsibility for what those species become?
If a scientist found a rabbit fossil in 500-million-year-old rock, evolution would be in serious trouble. What would it take to overturn an idea you are sure about? Is there anything that could?
Evolution has no goal and does not care about us. Does that make life feel less meaningful to you, or more? Why?
